entries.entry: Mathematical Proof (Pedagogical Strategy): Never state a theorem without intuition. Guide the student step by step: 1) State what is given clearly; 2) Identify the exact target condition; 3) Test small boundary cases (n=1, n=2); 4) Choose the appropriate proof method (Direct, Contradiction, Induction, or Invariance); 5) Conclude clearly with Q.E.D. Check each logical bridge.

Calculus (Pedagogical Strategy): Anchor mathematical abstractions to geometric and physical motion. Explain limits as dynamic approach, not static substitution. Highlight continuity as unbroken transitions, and show how infinite smallness produces exact macroscopic answers.

Derivatives & Rates of Change (Pedagogical Strategy): 1) Visualize the secant line shrinking to the tangent slope Δy/Δx; 2) Explain physical velocity vs position; 3) Unpack operational rules (Product, Quotient, Chain Rule) using geometric area expansions rather than rote memorization.

Integrals & Accumulation (Pedagogical Strategy): 1) Frame integration as continuous summation of infinitesimal slices (Riemann rectangles); 2) Connect via Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Accumulation undoes Rate of Change); 3) When choosing techniques (u-substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions), inspect symmetries first.

Linear Algebra (Pedagogical Strategy): View matrices as geometric coordinate transformations (rotations, shears, scalings of grid space). Explain eigenvectors as special directions where vectors only stretch without rotating, and eigenvalues as their scaling factors.

Matrices & Systems of Equations (Pedagogical Strategy): 1) Frame rows as hyperplanes and columns as vector combinations; 2) Explain determinants as scaling factors of signed volume; 3) Solve systems step by step using elementary row operations, explaining what each row operation means geometrically.

Probability & Statistics (Pedagogical Strategy): 1) Define sample space and event space clearly; 2) Differentiate dependent vs independent events; 3) For Bayes' Theorem, draw a 2x2 contingency grid or tree diagram to make prior vs posterior intuitive before plugging into formulas.

Equations & Problem Solving (Pedagogical Strategy): 1) Identify the domain and constraints on variables; 2) Balance both sides systematically with invertible operations; 3) Verify candidate roots against extraneous solutions introduced by squaring or division by zero.
